action_criteria.expected_evidence: Right frontal 5.6 cm mass extending into the precentral gyrus with thick irregular nodular ring enhancement, central necrosis, rim restricted diffusion, extensive vasogenic edema and 9 mm leftward midline shift
action_criteria.label: Order MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol with DWI, FLAIR, post-contrast T1) to characterize the right frontal lesion, define mass effect, and plan surgery
action_criteria.rationale: Contrast MRI with a standardised tumour protocol characterises the lesion and its mass effect, identifies the target for tissue sampling and is required before surgery (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: rCBV ratio 3.6 in the enhancing rim, supporting a high-grade neoplasm and identifying the target for tissue sampling
action_criteria.label: Order MR perfusion imaging (DSC perfusion) to assess tumor vascularity and target highest-grade region for biopsy
action_criteria.rationale: Elevated rCBV supports a high-grade neoplasm and points to the most vascular region to sample; tissue decides the diagnosis (Law 2003).

action_criteria.rationale: Raised choline with reduced NAA and lipid-lactate supports a high-grade neoplasm; it does not replace tissue (Bulik 2013).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No contraindication to surgery: normal blood count, platelets, electrolytes, renal and liver tests and coagulation; glucose 108 mg/dL; type and screen completed

action_criteria.rationale: Performance status selects the treatment branch after the integrated diagnosis; KPS below 70 is the unfavourable threshold (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Left-hand motor activation 8 mm from the enhancing margin; language left-lateralised with laterality index 0.77
action_criteria.label: Order functional MRI to map the left-hand motor cortex before resection of the precentral component
action_criteria.rationale: The tumour extends into the precentral gyrus with left arm weakness; functional MRI defines how much can be removed safely (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Right corticospinal tract displaced and continuous, 7 mm from the posterior enhancing margin
action_criteria.label: Order DTI tractography of the right corticospinal tract before resection
action_criteria.rationale: The corticospinal tract runs beneath the precentral component; tractography defines the subcortical limit of resection (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Integrated diagnosis Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4 with IDH1 R132H IHC negative, ATRX retained and MGMT promoter methylated, with TERT promoter mutation and EGFR amplification
action_criteria.label: Obtain tissue by maximal safe resection of the right frontal lesion, or stereotactic biopsy if resection is not safely feasible, for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis with IDH1 R132H immunohistochemistry, ATRX immunohistochemistry and MGMT promoter methylation
action_criteria.rationale: Surgery is the first option for a resectable glioma and should be as extensive as safely possible (AIOM; EANO 2021). Only tissue establishes the integrated diagnosis and the molecular results that select treatment; here resection also treats the mass effect.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Ibuprofen with dexamethasone raises gastrointestinal bleeding risk and should stop before surgery; sulfonamide allergy excludes co-trimoxazole for Pneumocystis prophylaxis

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform lumbar puncture: 9 mm midline shift with papilledema carries a risk of herniation
Do not initiate definitive tumor-directed therapy (radiation, temozolomide, alkylating chemotherapy) before tissue diagnosis is established
Do not start therapeutic anticoagulation without a clear thromboembolic indication, given upcoming neurosurgical intervention and bleeding risk
required_recommendations: Refer urgently to neurosurgery for maximal safe resection of the right frontal lesion, with preoperative functional MRI and DTI tractography and intraoperative mapping; send the specimen for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis (WHO CNS5).

Continue dexamethasone, started in the emergency department, for symptomatic vasogenic oedema at the lowest effective dose (for example 4 mg every 6 to 8 hours while mass effect is marked), with glucose monitoring and gastric protection, and taper after surgery.

Continue levetiracetam, started in the emergency department, for the documented focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure of left-hand onset and the preceding focal left-hand seizures; this is treatment of tumour-related epilepsy, not prophylaxis. Review the dose against seizure control and tolerance. Avoid enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital), which lower dexamethasone and chemotherapy exposure.
Stop ibuprofen and use paracetamol: with dexamethasone it raises the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding, and its antiplatelet effect should be off before surgery.

After the integrated diagnosis, refer to the neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team; for glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, at age 59 with KPS 70, radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide (Stupp 2005; EANO 2021), with Pneumocystis prophylaxis during the concomitant phase by an agent other than trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole because of his sulfonamide allergy, and effective contraception during and after temozolomide.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Paolo Feretti is a 59-year-old right-handed man and avid amateur cyclist who presents to the emergency department following a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. His wife reports that approximately four weeks ago he began experiencing intermittent tingling and burning pain in his left hand and forearm. Initially, he and his general practitioner attributed these symptoms to nerve compression related to prolonged cycling posture on his road bike, and he was referred for physiotherapy. Over the following two weeks, the paresthesias became more frequent and intense, occurring not only during cycling but also at rest, and were accompanied by brief involuntary twitching movements of his left hand lasting seconds at a time. Three weeks ago, he developed a progressive right-sided headache that was worst in the early morning hours and occasionally woke him from sleep. Over-the-counter ibuprofen provided only partial relief. Approximately two weeks ago, his wife began noticing that he had difficulty using his left hand for fine motor tasks such as buttoning shirts and typing on his keyboard. He also appeared more forgetful and slower in his thinking over the past ten days, occasionally losing track of conversations and misplacing items. This morning at approximately 08:30, while sitting at the breakfast table, his wife witnessed his left hand begin to assume a tonic posture, followed within seconds by rhythmic clonic jerking that spread to involve the entire left arm and then progressed to a generalized convulsion lasting approximately 75 seconds. He was confused and somnolent for about ten minutes afterward. EMS was called and he was transported to the emergency department. On arrival, he was alert and conversant but had a persistent right-sided headache and mild left arm weakness. He denies any prior seizure history, recent head trauma, fever, vision changes, nausea, or vomiting. He reports no recent weight loss or night sweats. A non-contrast CT scan obtained in the emergency department demonstrated a large heterogeneously hyperdense mass in the right frontal lobe with significant surrounding hypodensity suggestive of vasogenic edema and approximately 9 mm of leftward midline shift. He was started on intravenous dexamethasone and levetiracetam, and admitted to the neurology service for further evaluation.
